explanations.14: This syntax sets AI_BLOG_DIR to the value of the environment variable if it exists, or defaults to ~/repositories/blog if it doesn't — the colon-equals is bash's way of saying "use this value or fall back to that one".
explanations.35: The [[ -t 1 ]] test checks if file descriptor 1 (standard output) is connected to a terminal; if it is, the output can be formatted with colors and hyperlinks, otherwise it's plain text.
explanations.36: This printf uses ANSI escape codes (the \e sequences) to create a clickable hyperlink that works in modern terminals, along with green color and underline formatting for the link text.
explanations.37: The ${1:t} is a zsh-specific parameter expansion that extracts just the tail (filename part) of the URL in $1, so a full path like /home/user/file.md becomes just file.md.
explanations.62: The ${RANDOM}${RANDOM}-$$ creates a unique session ID by combining two random numbers and the process ID, ensuring each query goes to a fresh conversation thread instead of reusing old answers.
explanations.71: This uses jq's // operator to extract the error field from the JSON response if it exists, or return empty if there's no error — it's a safe way to check for problems.
explanations.81: This jq filter selects sources that have a chunkSource field starting with "link://", then removes that prefix and keeps only unique URLs, finally formatting each as url and title separated by a tab character.
explanations.90: The ${(f)sources} is zsh syntax that splits the sources string by newlines into separate words; the for loop then iterates over each line.
explanations.91: This extracts the first tab-separated field (${line%%$'\t'*}) and the second field (${line#*$'\t'}) from each source line to pass them as URL and title to the link function.
explanations.102: The noglob alias tells zsh to disable glob pattern matching for this command, so question marks and asterisks are passed literally to the function instead of being expanded as wildcards.
explanations.128: This complex parameter expansion converts the question to lowercase (L), removes non-alphanumeric characters, splits it into words, and removes duplicates — creating a list of candidate search terms.
explanations.134: The ceiling variable is set to one-tenth of the total blog posts, with a minimum of 3; it's used later to filter out keywords that match too many posts to be meaningful.
explanations.140: This skips any candidate word shorter than 4 characters, since very short words are unlikely to be meaningful topic keywords.
explanations.161: Using sed instead of awk with -F because article titles often contain colons, and awk's field separator would split on those and break the parsing.
